# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# unicode_normalization - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unicode-normalization/^0.1.22/

## Expand description

Unicode character composition and decomposition utilities
as described in
[Unicode Standard Annex #15](http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/).

```
extern crate unicode_normalization;
use unicode_normalization::char::compose;
use unicode_normalization::UnicodeNormalization;
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(compose('A','\u{30a}'), Some('Å'));
    let s = "ÅΩ";
    let c = s.nfc().collect::<String>();
    assert_eq!(c, "ÅΩ");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cratesio)crates.io

You can use this package in your project by adding the following
to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
unicode-normalization = "0.1.20"
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Methods for composing and decomposing characters.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Decompositions](https://docs.rs/struct.Decompositions.html)
- External iterator for a string decomposition’s characters.
- [Recompositions](https://docs.rs/struct.Recompositions.html)
- External iterator for a string recomposition’s characters.
- [Replacements](https://docs.rs/struct.Replacements.html)
- External iterator for replacements for a string’s characters.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamSafe.html)- Safe
- [UAX15-D4](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/#UAX15-D4): This iterator keeps track of how many non-starters there have been since the last starter in- *NFKD*and will emit a Combining Grapheme Joiner (U+034F) if the count exceeds 30.

`Maybe`

- Authoritatively check if a string is in NFC.

# zeroize - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/^1.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-zeroize)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto): zeroize

Securely zero memory (a.k.a. [zeroize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeroisation)) while avoiding compiler optimizations.

This crate implements a portable approach to securely zeroing memory using techniques which guarantee they won’t be “optimized away” by the compiler.

The [ Zeroize trait](https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/trait.Zeroize.html) is the crate’s primary API.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

[Zeroing memory securely is hard](http://www.daemonology.net/blog/2014-09-04-how-to-zero-a-buffer.html) - compilers optimize for performance, and
in doing so they love to “optimize away” unnecessary zeroing calls. There are
many documented “tricks” to attempt to avoid these optimizations and ensure
that a zeroing routine is performed reliably.

This crate isn’t about tricks: it uses [core::ptr::write_volatile](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.write_volatile.html)
and [core::sync::atomic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/core/sync/atomic/index.html) memory fences to provide easy-to-use, portable
zeroing behavior which works on all of Rust’s core number types and slices
thereof, implemented in pure Rust with no usage of FFI or assembly.

- No insecure fallbacks!
- No dependencies!
- No FFI or inline assembly! **WASM friendly**(and tested)!
- `#![no_std]`i.e.- **embedded-friendly**!
- No functionality besides securely zeroing memory!
- (Optional) Custom derive support for zeroing complex structures

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Requires Rust **1.85** or newer.

In the future, we reserve the right to change MSRV (i.e. MSRV is out-of-scope for this crate’s semantic versioning guarantees).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// Protip: don't embed secrets in your source code.
// This is just an example.
let mut secret = b"Air shield password: 1,2,3,4,5".to_vec();
// [ ... ] open the air shield here
// Now that we're done using the secret, zero it out.
secret.zeroize();
```

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#traits)Traits

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is the core API of this crate. It’s intended to be impl’d on values that
may-or-may-not contain secrets, for example the

`zeroize` crate itself defines them on the
core integers e.g. `u8`, `u16`, `i8`, `i16`, as well as arrays thereof. Its core API is
[, a method which takes](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html#tymethod.zeroize)

`Zeroize::zeroize``&mut self` and writes over the type’s internal
memory with some placeholder value, typically some form of `0`.The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which have a

[impl that can be used for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[. Types which implement this trait receive a blanket impl of the](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`We recommend that types which always contain secrets, and especially ones which need to maintain
complex invariants, do NOT impl the [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait, but instead provide a

[impl which takes care of erasing the secret values from memory directly. Such types can mark that they’re doing this with the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[marker trait. Note that](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`[is](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`*just*a marker trait, and making it actually work requires actually providing a

[impl which takes care of zeroizing secrets.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`Why not impl [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for such types, e.g. a

`SecretKey` type? The problem is [would effectively leave such types in an invalid state, and a sort of use-after-zeroize condition becomes possible. For that reason, we recommend these types automatically handle zeroization in their](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[handler alone.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[§](https://docs.rs#supported-types)Supported types

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is impl’d on all of Rust’s core scalar types including
integers, floats,

`bool`, and `char`.Additionally, it’s implemented on slices and `IterMut`s of the above types.

When the `alloc` feature is enabled (which it is by default), it’s also
impl’d for `Vec<T>` for the above types as well as `String`, where it provides
[ Vec::clear](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.clear) /

[-like behavior (truncating to zero-length) but ensures the backing memory is securely zeroed with some caveats.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.clear)

`String::clear`With the `std` feature enabled (which it is **not** by default), [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)
is also implemented for

[. After calling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.CString.html)

`CString``zeroize()` on a `CString`,
its internal buffer will contain exactly one nul byte. The backing
memory is zeroed by converting it to a `Vec<u8>` and back into a `CString`.
(NOTE: see “Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes” for important `Vec`/`String`/`CString` details)The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which also
impl

[, which implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[by overwriting a value with the default value.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derive-support)Custom Derive Support

This crate has custom derive support for the `Zeroize` trait,
gated under the `zeroize` crate’s `zeroize_derive` Cargo feature,
which automatically calls `zeroize()` on all members of a struct
or tuple struct.

Attributes supported for `Zeroize`:

On the item level:

- `#[zeroize(drop)]`:- *deprecated*use- `ZeroizeOnDrop`instead
- `#[zeroize(bound = "T: MyTrait")]`: this replaces any trait bounds inferred by zeroize

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Attributes supported for `ZeroizeOnDrop`:

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Example which derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::{Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop};
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which does not derive `Drop` (useful for e.g. `Copy` types)

```
#[cfg(feature = "zeroize_derive")]
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// This struct will *NOT* be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroize)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which only derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop;
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zeroizingz-wrapper-for-zeroizing-arbitrary-values-on-drop)`Zeroizing<Z>`: wrapper for zeroizing arbitrary values on drop

`Zeroizing<Z: Zeroize>` is a generic wrapper type that impls `Deref`
and `DerefMut`, allowing access to an inner value of type `Z`, and also
impls a `Drop` handler which calls `zeroize()` on its contents:

```
use zeroize::Zeroizing;
fn use_secret() {
    let mut secret = Zeroizing::new([0u8; 5]);
    // Set the air shield password
    // Protip (again): don't embed secrets in your source code.
    secret.copy_from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    assert_eq!(secret.as_ref(), &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    // The contents of `secret` will be automatically zeroized on drop
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-guarantees-does-this-crate-provide)What guarantees does this crate provide?

This crate guarantees the zeroing operation can’t be “optimized away” by the compiler, as ensured by LLVM’s volatile semantics.

Previously there were worries that the approach used by this crate (mixing volatile and
non-volatile accesses) was undefined behavior due to language contained
in the documentation for `write_volatile`, however after some discussion
within the [Unsafe Code Guidelines Working Group](https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines), [these remarks have been removed](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/60972) and the
specific usage pattern in this crate is considered to be well-defined.

All of that said, there is still potential for microarchitectural attacks (ala Spectre/Meltdown) to leak “zeroized” secrets through covert channels. This crate makes no guarantees that zeroized values cannot be leaked through such channels, as they represent flaws in the underlying hardware.

[§](https://docs.rs#stackheap-zeroing-notes)Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes

This crate can be used to zero values from either the stack or the heap. We recommend storing sensitive data on the heap whenever possible to reduce the potential for making copies in memory via Rust move semantics, however note that stack spilling and other optimizations may leave temporary copies of data from the heap on the stack.

[ zeroize_stack](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_stack.html) can be used to zeroize stack memory.

[ Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html) can be leveraged in conjunction with this crate to ensure data kept
on the stack isn’t moved.

The `Zeroize` impls for `Vec`, `String` and `CString` zeroize the entire capacity of their
backing buffer, but cannot guarantee copies of the data were not previously made by buffer
reallocation. It’s therefore important when attempting to zeroize such buffers to initialize
them to the correct capacity, and take care to prevent subsequent reallocation.

The [ secrecy](https://docs.rs/secrecy) crate provides higher-level abstractions for eliminating
usage patterns which can cause reallocations:

[§](https://docs.rs#what-about-clearing-registers-mlock-mprotect-etc)What about: clearing registers, `mlock()`, `mprotect()`, etc?

This crate is focused on providing simple, unobtrusive support for reliably zeroing memory using the best approach possible on stable Rust.

Clearing registers is a difficult problem that can’t easily be solved by
something like a crate, and requires either inline ASM or rustc support.
See [https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046) for background on
this particular problem.

Other memory protection mechanisms are interesting and useful, but often overkill (e.g. defending against RAM scraping or attackers with swap access). In as much as there may be merit to these approaches, there are also many other crates that already implement more sophisticated memory protections. Such protections are explicitly out-of-scope for this crate.

Zeroing memory is [good cryptographic hygiene](https://github.com/veorq/cryptocoding#clean-memory-of-secret-data) and this crate seeks to promote
it in the most unobtrusive manner possible. This includes omitting complex
`unsafe` memory protection systems and just trying to make the best memory
zeroing crate available.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [optimization_](https://docs.rs/fn.optimization_barrier.html)- barrier

- [zeroize_](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_flat_type.html)- flat_ - type - ⚠
- Zeroizes a flat type/struct. Only zeroizes the values that it owns, and it does not work on
dynamically sized values or trait objects. It would be inefficient to use this function on a
type that already implements `ZeroizeOnDrop`.

- Zeroize `N`bytes of stack space.

# bip39 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bip39/latest/target-redirect/bip39/

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [core](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/index.html);
- `pub extern crate`- [crate_rand](https://docs.rs/rand/0.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/index.html)as rand;

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ambiguous](https://docs.rs/struct.AmbiguousLanguages.html)- Languages
- A structured used in the [Error::AmbiguousLanguages](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.AmbiguousLanguages)variant that iterates over the possible languages.
- [Mnemonic](https://docs.rs/struct.Mnemonic.html)
- A mnemonic code.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rand 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/0.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/index.html

# Rand

A Rust library for random number generation.

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

The core random number generation traits of Rand live in the [rand_core](https://crates.io/crates/rand_core) crate but are also exposed here; RNG
implementations should prefer to use `rand_core` while most other users should
depend on `rand`.

Documentation:

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.6"
```
To get started using Rand, see [The Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book/).

## Versions

The Rand lib is not yet stable, however we are careful to limit breaking changes and warn via deprecation wherever possible. Patch versions never introduce breaking changes. The following minor versions are supported:

- Version 0.6 was released in November 2018, redesigning the `seq`module, moving most PRNGs to external crates, and many small changes.
- Version 0.5 was released in May 2018, as a major reorganisation
(introducing `RngCore`and`rand_core`, and deprecating`Rand`and the previous distribution traits).
- Version 0.4 was released in December 2017, but contained almost no breaking changes from the 0.3 series.

A detailed [changelog](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md) is available.

When upgrading to the next minor series (especially 0.4 → 0.5), we recommend
reading the [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html).

### Rust version requirements

Since version 0.5, Rand requires **Rustc version 1.22 or greater**.
Rand 0.4 and 0.3 (since approx. June 2017) require Rustc version 1.15 or
greater. Subsets of the Rand code may work with older Rust versions, but this
is not supported.

Travis CI always has a build with a pinned version of Rustc matching the oldest supported Rust release. The current policy is that this can be updated in any Rand release if required, but the change must be noted in the changelog.

To avoid bumping the required version unnecessarily, we use a `build.rs` script
to auto-detect the compiler version and enable certain features or change code
paths automatically. Since this makes it easy to unintentionally make use of
features requiring a more recent Rust version, we recommend testing with a
pinned version of Rustc if you require compatibility with a specific version.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with only the `std` feature enabled by default. The following
optional features are available:

- `alloc`can be used instead of- `std`to provide- `Vec`and- `Box`.
- `log`enables some logging via the- `log`crate.
- `nightly`enables all unstable features (- `simd_support`).
- `serde1`enables serialization for some types, via Serde version 1.
- `simd_support`enables uniform sampling of SIMD types (integers and floats).
- `stdweb`enables support for- `OsRng`on- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`via- `stdweb`combined with- `cargo-web`.
- `wasm-bindgen`enables support for- `OsRng`on- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`via- `wasm-bindgen`

`no_std` mode is activated by setting `default-features = false`; this removes
functionality depending on `std`:

- `thread_rng()`, and- `random()`are not available, as they require thread-local storage and an entropy source.
- `OsRng`and- `EntropyRng`are unavailable.
- `JitterRng`code is still present, but a nanosecond timer must be provided via- `JitterRng::new_with_timer`
- Since no external entropy is available, it is not possible to create
generators with fresh seeds using the `FromEntropy`trait (user must provide a seed).
- Several non-linear distributions distributions are unavailable since `exp`and`log`functions are not provided in`core`.
- Large parts of the `seq`-uence module are unavailable, unless the`alloc`feature is used (several APIs and many implementations require`Vec`).

# License

Rand is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.210/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs/](https://serde.rs/) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Helper macro when implementing the`Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A**data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- A**data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- A**data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- A**data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- Derive macro available if serde is built with`features = ["derive"]`.
- Derive macro available if serde is built with`features = ["derive"]`.

# bamboo_subagent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-subagent/2026.7.3/bamboo_subagent/

## Expand description

`bamboo-subagent` — sub-agent fleet runtime.

Slice 1 (this build): pure filesystem logic, no runtime dependency.

- `store`
- `mailbox`

See `docs/subagent-actor-runtime-design.md` (§3.4, §5) and
`docs/subagent-store-mailbox-interface.md` for the design these implement.

The session payload is kept opaque (generic `T: Serialize`/`DeserializeOwned`) so this
crate stays a leaf and is fully unit-testable with a tempdir; higher layers pass the
domain `Session`. Index rebuild is decoupled via the [ store::MetaExtractor](https://docs.rs/store/trait.MetaExtractor.html) seam.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use discovery::`- [Discovery](https://docs.rs/discovery/trait.Discovery.html);
- `pub use discovery::`- [Fabric](https://docs.rs/discovery/struct.Fabric.html);
- `pub use discovery::`- [FileFabric](https://docs.rs/discovery/type.FileFabric.html);

# ikigai_rdf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-rdf/0.1.3/ikigai_rdf/

## Expand description

`ikigai-rdf` — RDF **transreption** as an ikigai resource.

`urn:rdf:transrept` takes an RDF document and re-serializes it into another syntax,
chosen by the `as` argument (content negotiation): Turtle, N-Triples, N-Quads, TriG,
RDF/XML, JSON-LD, or a human-readable HTML table. The input syntax is sniffed (an
explicit format isn’t needed for the common cases).

It’s the first step toward NetKernel-style *transreption* — lossless transformation
between representations of the same resource. Built on Oxigraph’s **pure** parser/
serializer crates (`oxrdfio`/`oxrdf`) — no store, no rocksdb — so it compiles to
`wasm32` and the browser can transrept a fetched graph **client-side**:

`source urn:httpGet url=https://example.org/thing | urn:rdf:transrept as=text/turtle`The kernel pipes the fetched bytes into `content`; `as` picks the representation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- [subclass_](https://docs.rs/fn.subclass_axioms.html)- axioms
- Parse a Turtle alignment graph and return every `rdfs:subClassOf`axiom as a`(subclass, superclass)`IRI pair — the closure pairs a host feeds to the kernel’s type-aware action selection (`Kernel::with_subclass_axioms`), so an entity typed`foaf:Person`satisfies a`schema:Person`action. Best-effort: triples whose subject or object isn’t an IRI (blank nodes, literals) and any unparseable triples are skipped —`subClassOf`relates named classes.

# ikigai_org - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-org/0.1.0/ikigai_org/

## Expand description

`ikigai-org` — the org-mode agenda as ROC resources.

`urn:org:agenda:{period}` reads **date-fixed events** (headlines with active
`<…>` timestamps, repeaters expanded into the window) from org files and
serves them as text or as the **same skolemized Turtle event graph**
`urn:personal:calendar` speaks — so org and native calendars union and diff
as graphs (the Brian-Busy materialized-view plan).

The org files are read **through the kernel**: the host binds them (e.g. an
`ikigai-fs` space jailed to the org directory at `urn:orgfile:{path}`) and
hands this space their IRIs. That keeps this crate free of filesystem
access — capability-gated, wasm-clean, and golden-thread-ready when the
host’s file space is cacheable.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-parsed-v1)What is parsed (v1)

Headlines (`* Title`) whose section carries an active timestamp:
`<YYYY-MM-DD [Day] [HH:MM[-HH:MM]] [+N{d,w,m,y}]>`. Inactive `[…]`
timestamps are ignored. Untimed stamps are all-day; a timed stamp without
an end defaults to one hour. Repeaters (`+1w`, `+1y`, …) are expanded into
the requested window.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agenda](https://docs.rs/struct.AgendaEndpoint.html)- Endpoint
- `urn:org:agenda[:{period}]`— the org agenda for a period (default- `week`), sourced through the kernel from the configured org-file resources.
- [OrgEvent](https://docs.rs/struct.OrgEvent.html)
- One agenda event, normalized. The same shape the calendar side speaks.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [agenda_](https://docs.rs/fn.agenda_events.html)- events
- Parse org text into the events overlapping `[win_start, win_end)`, expanding repeaters into the window.
- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- Mount the agenda: `urn:org:agenda`and`urn:org:agenda:{period}`, reading the given org-file resources through the kernel.

# bamboo_a2a - Rust

## Expand description

Implements the Google A2A v1.0 specification:

Source: https://docs.rs/pdfmuse-core/0.1.6/pdfmuse_core/

## Expand description

pdfmuse-core — deterministic PDF/DOCX parser core.

The naive `parse()` lands in PER-33 and the self-written content-stream
interpreter (the real value) in PER-36. The unified IR — the data foundation
that every binding serializes byte-identically — lives in [ ir](https://docs.rs/ir/index.html).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use error::`- [PdfmuseError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.PdfmuseError.html);
- `pub use error::`- [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- Pluggable vision backend — the ML boundary.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Structured error type.
- [ir](https://docs.rs/ir/index.html)
- Unified intermediate representation (IR).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/struct.Chunk.html)
- A retrieval unit: a block’s text plus the context needed to cite it.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [chunk](https://docs.rs/fn.chunk.html)
- Split `doc`into chunks (one per non-empty block), tracking heading context.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parse `data`into the unified`ir::Document`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_with_password.html)- with_ - password
- Like `parse``password`for encrypted PDFs.
- [to_json](https://docs.rs/fn.to_json.html)
- Serialize the entire `Document`
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_markdown.html)- markdown
- Render `doc`to GitHub-flavored Markdown, pages and blocks in order.
- [to_text](https://docs.rs/fn.to_text.html)
- Render `doc`to plain reading-order text — no Markdown syntax, just the block text joined by newlines. The cheapest useful output for search / ATS / feeding an LLM, and (via the bindings) avoids materializing the full IR on the host.

**facett-timeline** — a **swimlane Gantt**: a wall-clock time axis with stacked,

engine-agnostic [ TimelineModel](https://docs.rs/model/struct.TimelineModel.html) (a host maps Spark’s
event log / REST API onto it; this crate never learns what a “stage” is).

- `model`- `[t0,t1]`window) with its own offset/- `state_json`tests.

- `Msg`- `TimelineView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter, the headless- `layout`- `state_json`all read bar offsets from- **one**formula (- `TimelineModel::bar_fraction_in`

# facett_tabbar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-tabbar/0.1.10/facett_tabbar/

## Expand description

**facett-tabbar** — the generic, themed **nav toolbar**: a control strip
(workspace/palette/About/live-style pickers + toggles, host-painted) plus a
two-row strip of tab headers, the active tab carrying the palette accent.
Adopted from nornir’s `src/viz/facett_ui.rs` (`TabBar` / `TabItem` /
`BarControl`) — the header of that file explicitly says it “should live in
the upstream `facett` crate”; the only thing that kept it in nornir is the
egui 0.33↔0.34 skew (egui-snarl pins 0.33). facett is on egui 0.34, so this
is the re-home; nornir re-points to `facett::tabbar::TabBar` once its viz
bumps to 0.34 (still gated on egui-snarl shipping 0.34 — see the cut policy
note in the batch report).

Two surfaces:

- `TabBar`- `&[TabItem]`+ an- `active`id), the verbatim port of nornir’s bar.- `show()`returns the id of the newly-clicked tab;- `state_json()`reports the tabs/active/split/controls.
- `TabBarView`- **owning**canonical- `Facet`- `local()`/- `remote()`,- `state_json()`,- `caps()`) so a- `FacetDeck`mounts the bar as a tab and a headless driver reads + drives the selection. It tracks its own- `active`and clicking a header re-keys it (and records the click count).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BarControl](https://docs.rs/struct.BarControl.html)
- A declarative descriptor of one **picker / toggle / button**the bar hosts in its left/right slots (workspace combo, palette combo, About toggle, live checkbox, …). The bar does NOT paint these — the host paints them through a slot closure — but the descriptor lets`state_json`report*which*controls are present and their values (the “components expose readable data” LAW) without the bar knowing anything domain-specific.
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBar.html)
- The generic, themed **nav/toolbar**widget: a control strip plus a two-row strip of tab headers, all painted in the active`Theme``&[TabItem]`, the left/right slots are host-supplied closures, and the controls they host are declared as`BarControl`
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBarView.html)- View
- An **owning**canonical`Facet``TabBar``tabs`+`active`+`controls`, paints the bar (no host slots — the controls are reported, not interactive here), tracks the live selection across frames, and exposes the whole rendered bar through`Facet::state_json`
- [TabItem](https://docs.rs/struct.TabItem.html)
- One tab in a `TabBar``id`(emitted in`state_json`+ matched on click) plus the human`label`egui paints on the header (icon + words, e.g.`"🔗 Dep Graph"`), so an AccessKit/robot click resolves by the same string the user reads. Keeping`id`and`label`separate lets a host rename a label without breaking click-by-id wiring or the`state_json`contract.
- [Underline](https://docs.rs/struct.UnderlineTween.html)- Tween
- Active-tab **underline slide**state (injected-clock, FC-7): holds the current eased underline rect, which each frame eases toward the active tab’s rect. Held by the owning`TabBarView``TabBar::show_anim`

# facett_syschart - Rust

## Expand description

**facett-syschart** — a **system-map chart**: a handful of *free-positioned*
peer nodes (not a layered DAG) joined by edges, each carrying a **badge**
(a count / status number) and, when selected, an **inline expandable detail
panel**. Click a node to select it; its detail renders in a panel under the
canvas. The host owns *what* a node’s detail is (a string here; richer hosts
draw their own widgets after `ui()` keyed off [ SystemChart::selected](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html#method.selected)).

This is the piece [ facett_core::draw](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/fn.draw.html)/[

`facett_graph::GraphView`] don’t
cover — those paint a *non-interactive*

`Scene`; `DepGraphView` is a
*layered*DAG with a fixed deps/dependents drill-down. A “monitoring map” of a few peer systems (a PKI/OIDC/Nexus triangle, a service mesh) wants deterministic positions, a per-node badge, click-select, and a free-form detail panel — that’s

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html)

`SystemChart`Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html):

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json` (every node, badge, edge + the selection), so it drops into a
`FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through `facett_core::harness` — drive
[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html#method.select)

`SystemChart::select``state_json`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [SysEdge](https://docs.rs/struct.SysEdge.html)
- An undirected link between two node ids.
- [SysNode](https://docs.rs/struct.SysNode.html)
- One system in the map. Positions are **normalized**(`0.0..=1.0`of the canvas), so the layout is resolution-independent and deterministic — ideal for headless rendering and screenshots.
- [System](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html)- Chart
- The system-map chart: nodes + edges + the current selection.

## Expand description

**facett-stat** — the generic, *non-domain* viz stat widgets factored out of

sparklines) and the inline-bar stat table from `src/viz/mcp_tab.rs`. The
nornir originals lived in the viz crate only because of an egui-version skew
(the viz is pinned to egui 0.33 by `egui-snarl`, facett is on 0.34) — the
header of `facett_ui.rs` says verbatim *“These widgets … should live in the
upstream  facett crate”*. facett is already on 0.34, so this is the re-home.

Two layers:

- **Free painter helpers**—- `status_verdict`- `sparkline`- `health_pill`- `egui::Painter`
- `StatGridView`- `Facet`- `StatRow`- `local()`/- `remote()`/- `state_json()`/- `caps()`so the deck + test matrix discover it.

- The amber used for running/stalled verdicts + the mid health band.

- A 0–100 **health pill**on a red→amber→green ramp. Port of nornir’s`viz::facett_ui::health_pill`(its`Theme::health_color`ramp inlined here so the widget is self-contained — facett-core’s`Theme`carries no health ramp).
- [sparkline](https://docs.rs/fn.sparkline.html)
- A tiny themed **sparkline**of a value series (line = palette`point`). Values self-normalize; higher = up. No-op for <2 points. Direct port of nornir’s`viz::facett_ui::sparkline`.
- [status_](https://docs.rs/fn.status_verdict.html)- verdict
- `(tag, colour)`for a free-text status on the active theme — the direct port of nornir’s- `viz::facett_ui::status_chip`. An unknown status is- `("?", dim)`.

# facett_plotters - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plotters/0.1.10/facett_plotters/

## Expand description

**facett-plotters** — the chart types [ egui_plot](https://docs.rs/egui_plot)
(→

`facett-plot`) *lacks*, painted in

**immediate mode**directly on an

[.](https://docs.rs/egui/0.34.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/egui/painter/struct.Painter.html)

`egui::Painter``egui_plot` already covers line/scatter/bar/histogram with
zoom/pan; this crate fills the analytics long-tail Plotly defines:- `BoxPlotView`
- `ViolinView`
- `HeatmapView`
- `CandlestickView`
- `TreemapView`

[§](https://docs.rs#why-hand-rolled-not-the-plotters-crate)Why hand-rolled, not the `plotters` crate

The `plotters` crate is **retained + raster/SVG-backend driven**: its egui
integration renders to a bitmap and blits a texture every frame, with no
immediate-mode hit-testing, no live theming, and no hover model. facett’s
charts must read [`facett_core::theme`] live (re-skin on theme switch),
expose cheap hover-readouts, and implement the [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)
contract (

`caps()` + `copy()` → CSV). Hand-painting on the egui `Painter`
(the same path `facett-core`/`facett-map` use) is the lighter, better-fitting
choice — so `plotters` is *not*a dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#theme-derived-colour-ramps)Theme-derived colour ramps

No palette is hardcoded. [ ramp::Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html) builds a

**sequential**(

`bg`→`accent`→`glow`) or **diverging**(

`accent`→`text_dim`→`glow`) ramp
purely from the active [, so heatmaps/treemaps follow whatever theme is set.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/theme/struct.Theme.html)

`Theme`Each view is a [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html): it declares

`caps().themeable().copyable().resizable()`, paints itself, and `copy()`
emits the underlying data as CSV. The data→geometry math (quartiles, KDE
bins, OHLC mapping, heatmap cell layout, treemap squarify) lives in **pure, tested functions**that need no GPU.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use boxplot::`- [BoxPlotView](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.BoxPlotView.html);
- `pub use boxplot::`- [Quartiles](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.Quartiles.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [CandlestickView](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.CandlestickView.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [Ohlc](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.Ohlc.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [OhlcLayout](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.OhlcLayout.html);
- `pub use heatmap::`- [HeatmapView](https://docs.rs/heatmap/struct.HeatmapView.html);
- `pub use ramp::`- [Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [Tile](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.Tile.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [TreemapView](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.TreemapView.html);
- `pub use violin::`- [Density](https://docs.rs/violin/struct.Density.html);
- `pub use violin::`- [ViolinView](https://docs.rs/violin/struct.ViolinView.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [boxplot](https://docs.rs/boxplot/index.html)
- **Box plot**— quartiles + whiskers + outliers, one box per named group. The data→geometry math (- `Quartiles::from_sorted`- `Quartiles::compute`- `BoxPlotView`- `Facet`
- [candlestick](https://docs.rs/candlestick/index.html)
- **Candlestick**(OHLC) chart. Each bar is an open/high/low/close tuple drawn as a wick (high→low) + a body (open↔close), coloured up/down from theme colours. The price→pixel mapping (- `OhlcLayout`
- [heatmap](https://docs.rs/heatmap/index.html)
- **Heatmap**— a- `rows × cols`matrix painted as a colour grid using a theme-derived- `Ramp`- `cell_rect`
- [ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/index.html)
- **Theme-derived colour ramps.**No hardcoded palette: a sequential ramp is built from the theme’s- `bg`→- `accent`→- `glow`, and a diverging ramp from- `accent`(low) through a neutral midpoint to- `glow`(high). Charts call- `Ramp::at`- `t ∈ 0..=1`to map a scalar to a colour.
- [treemap](https://docs.rs/treemap/index.html)
- **Treemap**— weighted rectangles, area ∝ value, laid out by a deterministic- **slice-and-dice**algorithm that alternates split direction by depth-of-cut so the tiling stays readable. The layout (- `squarify`- `(index, Rect)`pairs, tested independently of any painter. Tile fills come from a theme-derived sequential- `Ramp`
- [violin](https://docs.rs/violin/index.html)
- **Violin plot**— a mirrored kernel-density silhouette per group. The KDE (- `kde`- `ViolinView`

# bip39 2.2.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bip39/2.2.2

# bip39

A Rust implementation of [BIP-39](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki)
mnemonic codes.

## Word lists (languages)

We support all languages
[specified in the BIP-39 standard](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/bip-0039-wordlists.md)
as of writing.

The English language is always loaded and other languages can be loaded using the corresponding feature.

Use the `all-languages` feature to enable all languages.

- English (always enabled)
- Simplified Chinese (`chinese-simplified`)
- Traditional Chinese (`chinese-traditional`)
- Czech (`czech`)
- French (`french`)
- Italian (`italian`)
- Japanese (`japanese`)
- Korean (`korean`)
- Portuguese (`portuguese`)
- Spanish (`spanish`)

## MSRV

This crate supports Rust v1.41.1 and up and works with `no_std`.

The `bitcoin_hashes` range dependency effects the MSRV as follows

- `bitcoin_hashes v0.12`: MSRV v1.41.1
- `bitcoin_hashes v0.13`: MSRV v1.48.0
- `bitcoin_hashes v0.14`: MSRV v1.56.0

When using older version of Rust, you might have to pin the versions of several crates, for an up-to-date list refer to [ contrib/test.sh](https://docs.rs/contrib/test.sh):

```
```
If you enable the `zeroize` feature the MSRV becomes 1.51.

---

# bip39 2.2.2 - Docs.rs

[115](#115)#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Copy)]
[117](#117)pub enum Error {
[118](#118)	BadWordCount(usize),
[120](#120)	UnknownWord(usize),
[124](#124)	BadEntropyBitCount(usize),
[126](#126)	InvalidChecksum,
[128](#128)	AmbiguousLanguages(AmbiguousLanguages),
[132](#132)}
[133](#133)
[134](#134)impl fmt::Display for Error {
[135](#135)	fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[136](#136)		match *self {
[137](#137)			Error::BadWordCount(c) => {
[138](#138)				write!(
[139](#139)					f,
[140](#140)					"mnemonic has an invalid word count: {}. Word count must be 12, 15, 18, 21, \
[141](#141)					or 24",
[142](#142)					c
[143](#143)				)
[144](#144)			}
[145](#145)			Error::UnknownWord(i) => write!(f, "mnemonic contains an unknown word (word {})", i,),
[146](#146)			Error::BadEntropyBitCount(c) => write!(
[147](#147)				f,
[148](#148)				"entropy was not between 128-256 bits or not a multiple of 32 bits: {} bits",
[149](#149)				c,
[150](#150)			),
[151](#151)			Error::InvalidChecksum => write!(f, "the mnemonic has an invalid checksum"),
[152](#152)			Error::AmbiguousLanguages(a) => {
[153](#153)				write!(f, "ambiguous word list: ")?;
[154](#154)				for (i, lang) in a.iter().enumerate() {
[155](#155)					if i == 0 {
[156](#156)						write!(f, "{}", lang)?;
[157](#157)					} else {
[158](#158)						write!(f, ", {}", lang)?;
[159](#159)					}
[160](#160)				}
[161](#161)				Ok(())
[162](#162)			}
[163](#163)		}
[164](#164)	}
[165](#165)}

[198](#198)	pub fn normalize_utf8_cow<'a>(cow: &mut Cow<'a, str>) {
[199](#199)		let is_nfkd = unicode_normalization::is_nfkd_quick(cow.as_ref().chars());
[200](#200)		if is_nfkd != unicode_normalization::IsNormalized::Yes {
[201](#201)			*cow = Cow::Owned(cow.as_ref().nfkd().to_string());
[202](#202)		}
[203](#203)	}
[204](#204)
[205](#205)	pub fn from_entropy_in(language: Language, entropy: &[u8]) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {
[208](#208)		const MAX_ENTROPY_BITS: usize = 256;
[209](#209)		const MIN_ENTROPY_BITS: usize = 128;
[210](#210)		const MAX_CHECKSUM_BITS: usize = 8;
[211](#211)
[212](#212)		let nb_bytes = entropy.len();
[213](#213)		let nb_bits = nb_bytes * 8;
[214](#214)
[215](#215)		if nb_bits % 32 != 0 {
[216](#216)			return Err(Error::BadEntropyBitCount(nb_bits));
[217](#217)		}
[218](#218)		if nb_bits < MIN_ENTROPY_BITS || nb_bits > MAX_ENTROPY_BITS {
[219](#219)			return Err(Error::BadEntropyBitCount(nb_bits));
[220](#220)		}
[221](#221)
[222](#222)		let check = sha256::Hash::hash(&entropy);
[223](#223)		let mut bits = [false; MAX_ENTROPY_BITS + MAX_CHECKSUM_BITS];
[224](#224)		for i in 0..nb_bytes {
[225](#225)			for j in 0..8 {
[226](#226)				bits[i * 8 + j] = (entropy[i] & (1 << (7 - j))) > 0;
[227](#227)			}
[228](#228)		}
[229](#229)		for i in 0..nb_bytes / 4 {
[230](#230)			bits[8 * nb_bytes + i] = (check[i / 8] & (1 << (7 - (i % 8)))) > 0;
[231](#231)		}
[232](#232)
[233](#233)		let mut words = [EOF; MAX_NB_WORDS];
[234](#234)		let nb_words = nb_bytes * 3 / 4;
[235](#235)		for i in 0..nb_words {
[236](#236)			let mut idx = 0;
[237](#237)			for j in 0..11 {
[238](#238)				if bits[i * 11 + j] {
[239](#239)					idx += 1 << (10 - j);
[240](#240)				}
[241](#241)			}
[242](#242)			words[i] = idx;
[243](#243)		}
[244](#244)
[245](#245)		Ok(Mnemonic {
[246](#246)			lang: language,
[247](#247)			words: words,
[248](#248)		})
[249](#249)	}
[250](#250)
[251](#251)	pub fn from_entropy(entropy: &[u8]) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {
[254](#254)		Mnemonic::from_entropy_in(Language::English, entropy)
[255](#255)	}

[257](#257)	#[cfg(feature = "rand_core")]
[270](#270)	pub fn generate_in_with<R>(
[271](#271)		rng: &mut R,
[272](#272)		language: Language,
[273](#273)		word_count: usize,
[274](#274)	) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error>
[275](#275)	where
[276](#276)		R: RngCore + CryptoRng,
[277](#277)	{
[278](#278)		if is_invalid_word_count(word_count) {
[279](#279)			return Err(Error::BadWordCount(word_count));
[280](#280)		}
[281](#281)
[282](#282)		let entropy_bytes = (word_count / 3) * 4;
[283](#283)		let mut entropy = [0u8; (MAX_NB_WORDS / 3) * 4];
[284](#284)		RngCore::fill_bytes(rng, &mut entropy[0..entropy_bytes]);
[285](#285)		Mnemonic::from_entropy_in(language, &entropy[0..entropy_bytes])
[286](#286)	}

[348](#348)	pub fn word_indices(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = usize> + Clone + '_ {

[367](#367)	fn language_of_iter<'a, W: Iterator<Item = &'a str>>(words: W) -> Result<Language, Error> {
[370](#370)		let mut words = words.peekable();
[371](#371)		let langs = Language::ALL;
[372](#372)		{
[373](#373)			let first_word = words.peek().ok_or(Error::BadWordCount(0))?;
[375](#375)			if first_word.len() == 0 {
[376](#376)				return Err(Error::BadWordCount(0));
[377](#377)			}
[378](#378)
[379](#379)			for language in langs.iter().filter(|l| l.unique_words()) {
[382](#382)				if language.find_word(first_word).is_some() {
[383](#383)					return Ok(*language);
[384](#384)				}
[385](#385)			}
[386](#386)		}
[387](#387)
[388](#388)		let mut possible = [false; language::MAX_NB_LANGUAGES];
[392](#392)		for (i, lang) in langs.iter().enumerate() {
[393](#393)			possible[i] = !lang.unique_words();
[396](#396)		}
[397](#397)		for (idx, word) in words.enumerate() {
[398](#398)			for (i, lang) in langs.iter().enumerate() {
[400](#400)				possible[i] &= lang.find_word(word).is_some();
[401](#401)			}
[402](#402)
[403](#403)			let mut iter = possible.iter().zip(langs.iter()).filter(|(p, _)| **p).map(|(_, l)| l);
[405](#405)
[406](#406)			match iter.next() {
[407](#407)				None => return Err(Error::UnknownWord(idx)),
[409](#409)				Some(remaining) => {
[411](#411)					if iter.next().is_none() {
[412](#412)						return Ok(*remaining);
[414](#414)					}
[415](#415)				}
[416](#416)			}
[417](#417)		}
[418](#418)
[419](#419)		return Err(Error::AmbiguousLanguages(AmbiguousLanguages(possible)));
[420](#420)	}
[421](#421)
[422](#422)	pub fn language_of<S: AsRef<str>>(mnemonic: S) -> Result<Language, Error> {
[433](#433)		Mnemonic::language_of_iter(mnemonic.as_ref().split_whitespace())
[434](#434)	}
[435](#435)
[436](#436)	pub fn parse_in_normalized(language: Language, s: &str) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {
[438](#438)		let nb_words = s.split_whitespace().count();
[439](#439)		if is_invalid_word_count(nb_words) {
[440](#440)			return Err(Error::BadWordCount(nb_words));
[441](#441)		}
[442](#442)
[443](#443)		let mut words = [EOF; MAX_NB_WORDS];
[445](#445)
[446](#446)		let mut bits = [false; MAX_NB_WORDS * 11];
[449](#449)
[450](#450)		for (i, word) in s.split_whitespace().enumerate() {
[451](#451)			let idx = language.find_word(word).ok_or(Error::UnknownWord(i))?;
[452](#452)
[453](#453)			words[i] = idx;
[454](#454)
[455](#455)			for j in 0..11 {
[456](#456)				bits[i * 11 + j] = idx >> (10 - j) & 1 == 1;
[457](#457)			}
[458](#458)		}
[459](#459)
[460](#460)		let mut entropy = [0u8; MAX_NB_WORDS / 3 * 4];
[463](#463)		let nb_bytes_entropy = nb_words / 3 * 4;
[464](#464)		for i in 0..nb_bytes_entropy {
[465](#465)			for j in 0..8 {
[466](#466)				if bits[i * 8 + j] {
[467](#467)					entropy[i] += 1 << (7 - j);
[468](#468)				}
[469](#469)			}
[470](#470)		}
[471](#471)		let check = sha256::Hash::hash(&entropy[0..nb_bytes_entropy]);
[472](#472)		for i in 0..nb_bytes_entropy / 4 {
[473](#473)			if bits[8 * nb_bytes_entropy + i] != ((check[i / 8] & (1 << (7 - (i % 8)))) > 0) {
[474](#474)				return Err(Error::InvalidChecksum);
[475](#475)			}
[476](#476)		}
[477](#477)
[478](#478)		Ok(Mnemonic {
[479](#479)			lang: language,
[480](#480)			words: words,
[481](#481)		})
[482](#482)	}
[483](#483)
[484](#484)	pub fn parse_in_normalized_without_checksum_check(
[490](#490)		language: Language,
[491](#491)		s: &str,
[492](#492)	) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {
[493](#493)		let nb_words = s.split_whitespace().count();
[494](#494)		if is_invalid_word_count(nb_words) {
[495](#495)			return Err(Error::BadWordCount(nb_words));
[496](#496)		}
[497](#497)
[498](#498)		let mut words = [EOF; MAX_NB_WORDS];
[500](#500)
[501](#501)		for (i, word) in s.split_whitespace().enumerate() {
[502](#502)			let idx = language.find_word(word).ok_or(Error::UnknownWord(i))?;
[503](#503)
[504](#504)			words[i] = idx;
[505](#505)		}
[506](#506)
[507](#507)		Ok(Mnemonic {
[508](#508)			lang: language,
[509](#509)			words: words,
[510](#510)		})
[511](#511)	}

[516](#516)		Mnemonic::parse_in_normalized(lang, s)

[532](#532)	pub fn parse<'a, S: Into<Cow<'a, str>>>(s: S) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {

[537](#537)			Language::ALL[0]

[550](#550)	pub fn to_seed_normalized(&self, normalized_passphrase: &str) -> [u8; 64] {

[553](#553)		const PBKDF2_BYTES: usize = 64;

[562](#562)	pub fn to_seed<'a, P: Into<Cow<'a, str>>>(&self, passphrase: P) -> [u8; 64] {
[563](#563)		let normalized_passphrase = {
[564](#564)			let mut cow = passphrase.into();
[565](#565)			Mnemonic::normalize_utf8_cow(&mut cow);

[571](#571)	pub fn to_entropy_array(&self) -> ([u8; 33], usize) {
[575](#575)		let language = Mnemonic::language_of_iter(self.words()).unwrap();
[579](#579)
[580](#580)		let mut entropy = [0; 33];
[582](#582)		let mut cursor = 0;
[583](#583)		let mut offset = 0;
[584](#584)		let mut remainder = 0;
[585](#585)
[586](#586)		let nb_words = self.word_count();
[587](#587)		for word in self.words() {
[588](#588)			let idx = language.find_word(word).expect("invalid mnemonic");
[589](#589)
[590](#590)			remainder |= ((idx as u32) << (32 - 11)) >> offset;
[591](#591)			offset += 11;
[592](#592)
[593](#593)			while offset >= 8 {
[594](#594)				entropy[cursor] = (remainder >> 24) as u8;
[595](#595)				cursor += 1;
[596](#596)				remainder <<= 8;
[597](#597)				offset -= 8;
[598](#598)			}
[599](#599)		}
[600](#600)
[601](#601)		if offset != 0 {
[602](#602)			entropy[cursor] = (remainder >> 24) as u8;
[603](#603)		}
[604](#604)
[605](#605)		let entropy_bytes = (nb_words / 3) * 4;
[606](#606)		(entropy, entropy_bytes)
[607](#607)	}
[608](#608)
[609](#609)	#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[611](#611)	pub fn to_entropy(&self) -> Vec<u8> {
[612](#612)		let (arr, len) = self.to_entropy_array();
[613](#613)		arr[0..len].to_vec()
[614](#614)	}
[615](#615)
[616](#616)	pub fn checksum(&self) -> u8 {
[639](#639)		let word_count = self.word_count();
[640](#640)		let last_word = self.words[word_count - 1];
[641](#641)		let mask = 0xFF >> (8 - word_count / 3);
[642](#642)		last_word as u8 & mask
[643](#643)	}
[644](#644)}
[645](#645)
[646](#646)impl fmt::Display for Mnemonic {
[647](#647)	fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[648](#648)		for (i, word) in self.words().enumerate() {
[649](#649)			if i > 0 {
[650](#650)				f.write_str(" ")?;
[651](#651)			}
[652](#652)			f.write_str(word)?;
[653](#653)		}
[654](#654)		Ok(())
[655](#655)	}
[656](#656)}
[657](#657)
[658](#658)impl fmt::Debug for Mnemonic {
[659](#659)	fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[660](#660)		f.debug_struct("Mnemonic")
[661](#661)			.field("lang", &self.language())
[662](#662)            .finish()
[664](#664)	}
[665](#665)}
[666](#666)
[667](#667)impl str::FromStr for Mnemonic {
[668](#668)	type Err = Error;
[669](#669)
[670](#670)	fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Mnemonic, Error> {
[671](#671)		#[cfg(feature = "unicode-normalization")]
[672](#672)		{
[673](#673)			Mnemonic::parse(s)
[674](#674)		}
[675](#675)		#[cfg(not(feature = "unicode-normalization"))]
[676](#676)		{
[677](#677)			Mnemonic::parse_normalized(s)
[678](#678)		}
[679](#679)	}
[680](#680)}
[681](#681)
[682](#682)fn is_invalid_word_count(word_count: usize) -> bool {
[683](#683)	word_count < MIN_NB_WORDS || word_count % 3 != 0 || word_count > MAX_NB_WORDS
[684](#684)}

[699](#699)				*lang,
[700](#700)				Mnemonic::language_of_iter(m.to_string().split_whitespace()).unwrap()
[701](#701)			);

[708](#708)	#[test]
[709](#709)	fn test_ambiguous_languages() {
[710](#710)		let mut present = [false; language::MAX_NB_LANGUAGES];
[711](#711)		let mut present_vec = Vec::new();
[712](#712)		let mut alternate = true;
[713](#713)		for i in 0..Language::ALL.len() {
[714](#714)			present[i] = alternate;
[715](#715)			if alternate {
[716](#716)				present_vec.push(Language::ALL[i]);
[717](#717)			}
[718](#718)			alternate = !alternate;
[719](#719)		}
[720](#720)		let amb = AmbiguousLanguages(present);
[721](#721)		assert_eq!(amb.to_vec(), present_vec);
[722](#722)		assert_eq!(amb.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), present_vec);
[723](#723)	}

[928](#928)		let vectors = [

[958](#958)		];
[959](#959)
[960](#960)		for entropy_hex in &vectors {
[961](#961)			let ent = Vec::from_hex(entropy_hex).unwrap();
[962](#962)			let m = Mnemonic::from_entropy(&ent).unwrap();
[963](#963)			let word_count = m.word_count();
[964](#964)			let cs = m.checksum();
[965](#965)			let digest = sha256::Hash::hash(&ent);
[966](#966)			dbg!(digest);
[967](#967)			assert_eq!(digest[0] >> (8 - word_count / 3), cs);
[968](#968)		}
[969](#969)	}
[970](#970)
[971](#971)	#[test]
[972](#972)	fn test_invalid_engish() {
[973](#973)		assert_eq!(
[977](#977)			Mnemonic::parse_normalized(
[978](#978)				"getter advice cage absurd amount doctor acoustic avoid letter advice cage above",
[979](#979)			),
[980](#980)			Err(Error::UnknownWord(0))
[981](#981)		);
[982](#982)
[983](#983)		assert_eq!(
[984](#984)			Mnemonic::parse_normalized(
[985](#985)				"letter advice cagex absurd amount doctor acoustic avoid letter advice cage above",
[986](#986)			),
[987](#987)			Err(Error::UnknownWord(2))
[988](#988)		);
[989](#989)
[990](#990)		assert_eq!(
[991](#991)			Mnemonic::parse_normalized(
[992](#992)				"advice cage absurd amount doctor acoustic avoid letter advice cage above",
[993](#993)			),
[994](#994)			Err(Error::BadWordCount(11))
[995](#995)		);
[996](#996)
[997](#997)		assert_eq!(
[998](#998)			Mnemonic::parse_normalized(
[999](#999)				"primary advice cage absurd amount doctor acoustic avoid letter advice cage above",
[1000](#1000)			),
[1001](#1001)			Err(Error::InvalidChecksum)
[1002](#1002)		);
[1003](#1003)	}

[1005](#1005)	#[test]
[1006](#1006)	fn test_invalid_entropy() {
[1007](#1007)		assert_eq!(Mnemonic::from_entropy(&vec![b'x'; 17]), Err(Error::BadEntropyBitCount(136)));
[1009](#1009)
[1010](#1010)		assert_eq!(Mnemonic::from_entropy(&vec![b'x'; 4]), Err(Error::BadEntropyBitCount(32)));
[1012](#1012)
[1013](#1013)		assert_eq!(Mnemonic::from_entropy(&vec![b'x'; 36]), Err(Error::BadEntropyBitCount(288)));
[1015](#1015)	}

[1017](#1017)	#[test]
[1018](#1018)	fn debug_does_not_leak_phrase() {
[1019](#1019)		let m = Mnemonic::from_entropy(&[0u8; 16]).unwrap();
[1020](#1020)
[1021](#1021)		let dbg = format!("{:?}", m);
[1022](#1022)
[1023](#1023)		assert!(dbg.starts_with("Mnemonic {") || dbg.starts_with("Mnemonic(") || dbg.contains("Mnemonic"),
[1024](#1024)			"Debug output doesn't look like a struct: {}", dbg);
[1025](#1025)		assert!(dbg.contains("lang"), "Debug must include language info: {}", dbg);
[1026](#1026)
[1027](#1027)		for w in m.words() {
[1028](#1028)			assert!(
[1029](#1029)				!dbg.contains(w),
[1030](#1030)				"Debug leaked sensitive word: {} (output: {})",
[1031](#1031)				w, dbg
[1032](#1032)			);
[1033](#1033)		}
[1034](#1034)	}

[1193](#1193)		for vector in &vectors {
[1194](#1194)			let entropy = Vec::<u8>::from_hex(&vector.0).unwrap();
[1195](#1195)			let mnemonic_str = vector.1;
[1196](#1196)			let passphrase = vector.2;
[1197](#1197)			let seed = Vec::<u8>::from_hex(&vector.3).unwrap();
[1198](#1198)
[1199](#1199)			let mnemonic = Mnemonic::from_entropy_in(Language::Japanese, &entropy).unwrap();
[1200](#1200)
[1201](#1201)			assert_eq!(seed, &mnemonic.to_seed(passphrase)[..], "failed vector: {}", mnemonic_str);
[1202](#1202)			let rt = Mnemonic::parse_in(Language::Japanese, mnemonic.to_string())
[1203](#1203)				.expect(&format!("vector: {}", mnemonic_str));
[1204](#1204)			assert_eq!(seed, &rt.to_seed(passphrase)[..]);
[1205](#1205)
[1206](#1206)			let mnemonic = Mnemonic::parse_in(Language::Japanese, mnemonic_str)
[1207](#1207)				.expect(&format!("vector: {}", mnemonic_str));
[1208](#1208)			assert_eq!(seed, &mnemonic.to_seed(passphrase)[..], "failed vector: {}", mnemonic_str);
[1209](#1209)		}
[1210](#1210)	}
[1211](#1211)}

# Error in bip39 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bip39/2.2.2/bip39/enum.Error.html

```
pub enum Error {
    BadWordCount(
```
[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)),
    UnknownWord([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)),
    BadEntropyBitCount([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)),
    InvalidChecksum,
    AmbiguousLanguages([AmbiguousLanguages](https://docs.rs/struct.AmbiguousLanguages.html)),
}## Expand description

A BIP39 error.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BadWordCount)

### BadWordCount([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Mnemonic has a word count that is not a multiple of 6.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnknownWord)

### UnknownWord([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Mnemonic contains an unknown word.
Error contains the index of the word.
Use `mnemonic.split_whitespace().get(i)` to get the word.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BadEntropyBitCount)

### BadEntropyBitCount([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Entropy was not a multiple of 32 bits or between 128-256n bits in length.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidChecksum)

### InvalidChecksum

The mnemonic has an invalid checksum.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AmbiguousLanguages)

### AmbiguousLanguages([AmbiguousLanguages](https://docs.rs/struct.AmbiguousLanguages.html))

The mnemonic can be interpreted as multiple languages. Use the helper methods of the inner struct to inspect which languages are possible.

# Mnemonic in bip39 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bip39/2.2.2/bip39/struct.Mnemonic.html

`pub struct Mnemonic { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A mnemonic code.

The [core::str::FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) implementation will try to determine the language of the
mnemonic from all the supported languages. (Languages have to be explicitly enabled using
the Cargo features.)

Supported number of words are 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)
